w: Home of Manchester United since 1910, Old Trafford holds 74500 and is the largest club football stadium in the UK. Nicknamed the Theatre of Dreams by Bobby Charlton, it hosted matches at the 1966 World Cup and Euro 96. Record attendance: 76962, set in 1939 for an FA Cup semi-final between Wolves and Grimsby Town.
s: Man United's Theatre of Dreams since 1910
_facts: Capacity 74500, largest club ground in the UK
Hosted 1966 World Cup and Euro 96 matches
Record attendance 76962 in 1939 FA Cup semi-final

w: Home of Super Lig club Galatasaray, officially the Ali Sami Yen Sports Complex and branded Rams Park for sponsorship. Seats 53978 in the Seyrantepe quarter of Sariyer, on Istanbul's European side. First Turkish stadium to meet UEFA Euro 2016 bid requirements; Galatasaray won the league in their first full season here.
_facts: First Turkish stadium meeting UEFA Euro 2016 requirements
Named after club founder Ali Sami Yen

w: Built as the main venue for the 1972 Summer Olympics, seating 63118 today. Hosted the 1974 World Cup final and the Euro 1988 final, plus European Cup finals in 1979, 1993 and 1997. Home to Bayern Munich and 1860 Munich until Allianz Arena opened for 2006; still Munich's main athletics stadium.
_facts: Main venue for the 1972 Summer Olympics
Hosted the 1974 World Cup final and Euro 1988 final
Former home of Bayern Munich until Allianz Arena

w: Poland's national football stadium, seating 58580, built 2008-2011 on the former 10th-Anniversary Stadium site. Its retractable PVC roof unfolds from a spire above the pitch, inspired by Frankfurt's Commerzbank-Arena. Co-hosted Euro 2012 with Ukraine, staging the opening match, a quarter-final and a semi-final.
_facts: Capacity 58580, largest football stadium in Poland
Hosted Euro 2012 opening match, quarter-final and semi-final

w: Home of West Bromwich Albion since 1900, the first Football League ground built in the 20th century, completed in just four months. Seats 27087 in West Bromwich, Sandwell. At 551 feet above sea level it is the highest ground of any Premier League or Football League club. Record attendance: 64815, set in March 1937.
s: West Brom's home since 1900, England's highest
_facts: Home of West Bromwich Albion since 1900
Highest-altitude ground in English league football, 551 feet

w: Home of Cardiff City and the Wales national team since opening on 22 July 2009 with a friendly against Celtic. Seats 33280 in the Leckwith area, replacing Ninian Park as the club's ground. Also hosted Cardiff Blues rugby union until 2011-12. Second-largest stadium in Wales after the Millennium Stadium.
s: Cardiff City and Wales's Leckwith home
_facts: Home of Cardiff City and Wales national team

w: Built for Euro 2012, hosting three group-stage games, Arena Lviv seats 34915. Home to FC Lviv and Rukh Lviv, and since 2014 also used by Shakhtar Donetsk, displaced from Donetsk by the Russo-Ukrainian War.
s: Euro 2012 venue, now Shakhtar's wartime home
_facts: Euro 2012 host venue, three group games
Home of FC Lviv and Rukh Lviv
Used by Shakhtar Donetsk since 2014 due to war

w: Home of AS Monaco in the Fontvieille district, near the French border at Cap-d'Ail. Known for the nine arches at its away end, it doubles as an athletics venue hosting the Herculis Diamond League meet. Staged the UEFA Super Cup in 1986 and 1998-2012. Monaco's only football and athletics stadium.
s: AS Monaco's home, famed for nine arches
_facts: Hosts the Herculis Diamond League athletics meet
Known for nine arches at the away end

w: Home of Nottingham Forest since 1898, on the banks of the River Trent in West Bridgford. Capacity 30445, with plans to expand toward 45000 and eventually 52500. Hosted Euro 1996 matches. Just 300 yards from Notts County's Meadow Lane, the closest pair of professional football grounds in England.
_facts: 300 yards from Meadow Lane, closest English grounds

w: Home of Ipswich Town since 1884, expanded in the early 2000s from 22600 to over 30000, the largest football capacity in East Anglia. Hosted an England friendly against Croatia in 2003 plus youth internationals, athletics meetings and hockey. Record attendance 38010, set in March 1975 against Leeds United.
_facts: Largest football capacity in East Anglia

w: Multi-purpose indoor arena in Belgrade seating 18386, built for basketball, futsal, handball, judo, table tennis, tennis, volleyball and water polo, plus concerts. Floor area covers 48000 square metres, with an underground tunnel linking a smaller warm-up hall. Formerly in the European Arenas Association.
_facts: Hosts basketball, handball, volleyball, water polo

w: Home of RSC Anderlecht, officially the Constant Vanden Stock Stadium and branded Lotto Park for sponsorship. Hosted the Euro 1972 semi-final between Hungary and the Soviet Union. Capacity has shrunk from 40000 to 21500 seats after safety-driven reductions, on the border of Astrid Park.
_facts: Hosted Euro 1972 semi-final, Hungary v Soviet Union
Named for club figure Constant Vanden Stock

w: Home of Glentoran F.C. since 1892, sponsored as the BetMcLean Oval. Severely damaged in the 1941 Belfast Blitz, it stood unusable until 1949, with new stands added in 1953 and 2000. Capacity is now restricted to 6050. Has hosted Irish Cup finals, the County Antrim Shield and the Setanta Cup.
s: Glentoran's home since 1892, rebuilt after Blitz
_facts: Hosts Irish Cup and Setanta Cup finals

w: The largest stadium in Bosnia and Herzegovina, located in the Kosevo neighbourhood of Sarajevo. Also known as Kosevo Olympic Stadium, it hosted the opening ceremony of the 1984 Winter Olympics. Named, for football and other events hosted by FK Sarajevo, after club player Asim Ferhatovic Hase.
_facts: Largest stadium in Bosnia and Herzegovina
Home ground associated with FK Sarajevo
Named after player Asim Ferhatovic Hase

w: Home of Stade Rennais since its 1912 inauguration, rebuilt in 2001 to seat 29778. Roazhon is the Breton name for Rennes. Has hosted France men's and women's internationals, the 2016 Top 14 rugby semi-finals, and six matches of the 2019 FIFA Women's World Cup including a quarter-final.
_facts: Hosted six matches at the 2019 Women's World Cup

w: Indoor arena in Barcelona's Olympic Ring, designed by Arata Isozaki and opened in 1990. Seats up to 17960, the largest indoor arena by capacity in Spain. Hosted artistic gymnastics, handball and volleyball at the 1992 Summer Olympics; now used for concerts and a wide range of indoor sports and cultural events.
_facts: Capacity 17960, largest indoor arena in Spain
Hosted gymnastics, handball, volleyball at 1992 Olympics
Part of the Olympic Ring complex

w: Multipurpose indoor arena in Nanterre, opened October 2017 for rugby club Racing 92, replacing Stade Olympique Yves-du-Manoir. Billed as Europe's largest indoor arena, it seats 30681 for rugby or up to 45000 for concerts. Hosted swimming and water polo at the 2024 Paris Olympics.
s: Europe's largest indoor arena, near Paris
_facts: Home of rugby club Racing 92 since 2017
Hosted swimming and water polo, 2024 Olympics

w: Home of Primera Division club Rayo Vallecano in the Madrid district of Puente de Vallecas. Opened 10 May 1976 after construction that began in 1972, seating 14708. Also known by the names Estadio Teresa Rivero and Estadio Puente de Vallecas across its history.

The Estadio Municipal de Butarque, known for sponsorship reasons as the Ontime Butarque, is a multi-use stadium in Leganes, Spain. It is used primarily for football matches and currently serves as the home ground of CD Leganes, hosting the club's league fixtures.

Temporary arena in London's Olympic Park at Stratford, built for basketball at the 2012 Summer Olympics and Paralympics. Designed to be fully recyclable, it was dismantled in January 2013. Its seating was sold to Barnet owner Tony Kleanthous and reused in the construction of The Hive Stadium.
_facts: Built for 2012 Olympics and Paralympics basketball
Seating reused at The Hive Stadium

w: Built for mass displays of synchronized gymnastics in Prague's Strahov district, with a pitch three times the length and width of a football field. Capacity of 250000, only 56000 seated, once the second-largest sports venue ever built. Unused for competitive sport since 2019; now a Sparta Prague training centre.
s: Vast gymnastics arena on Petrin Hill
_facts: Once the second-largest sports venue ever built
Built for mass synchronized gymnastics displays
Now a Sparta Prague training centre

w: Temporary stadium built in London's Olympic Park, in Hackney Wick, for the 2012 Summer Olympics. Its pitch was a water-based astroturf, the surface used for Olympic field hockey competition, hosting matches during the London 2012 Games before the venue was later dismantled.
_facts: Located in the Olympic Park, Hackney Wick, London

w: Stadium in Rome along the Via Flaminia, three kilometres northwest of the city centre and 300 metres from the Parco di Villa Glori. Its interior spaces include a covered swimming pool and rooms for fencing, amateur wrestling, weightlifting, boxing and gymnastics, reflecting its multi-sport design.
s: Multi-sport stadium off the Via Flaminia
_facts: Located on the Via Flaminia, Rome
Houses rooms for fencing, wrestling, weightlifting, boxing, gymnastics

w: Multi-purpose stadium in the Rades suburb of Tunis, opened 2001 as the 7 November Stadium for the Mediterranean Games. Home to Tunisia's national team, Esperance de Tunis and Club Africain, it covers 13000 square metres and holds 60000. Hosted six matches of the 2004 Africa Cup of Nations, won by Tunisia.
_facts: Home of Esperance de Tunis, Club Africain, national team

w: Home of FC Utrecht since 1970, seating 23750 after renovation. Reopened in 1982 with a distinctive moat around the pitch, then among the most modern stadiums in the world. Hosted seven Netherlands national team matches and the 2005 FIFA U-20 World Cup final, won by Argentina over Nigeria.
_facts: Hosted 2005 FIFA U-20 World Cup final

w: The biggest indoor arena in Slovenia, located in Ljubljana's Bezigrad district as part of the Stozice Sports Park. Designed by Slovenian architecture firm Sadar + Vuga, it serves as the home ground of basketball club KK Cedevita Olimpija.
_facts: Home of basketball club KK Cedevita Olimpija
Part of the Stozice Sports Park complex

w: Home of Bohemian F.C. since the early 20th century in Phibsborough, Dublin, affectionately known to fans as Dalyer. Long regarded as the home of Irish football, it hosted many Irish international matches and FAI Cup finals, plus European qualifiers. Capacity 4443; largely undeveloped between the 1940s and 2000s.
_facts: Home of Bohemian F.C. since the early 20th century
Historic host of Irish internationals and FAI Cup finals

w: Home of Jagiellonia Bialystok, redeveloped and reopened at the end of 2014 with 22432 seats, also known as the Stadion Jagiellonii Bialystok. Redevelopment costs were disputed between the city and its Polish-French, then Spanish-Polish, contractors. Sponsored as the Chorten Arena since September 2024.

Home stadium of MTK Budapest in the Jozsefvaros district of Budapest, opened on 13 October 2016. Named after Nandor Hidegkuti, the MTK and Hungary forward who lived from 1922 to 2002, and seats 5322 spectators for club football matches.

Home of Plymouth Argyle since 1903, seating 17900 in Milehouse, Plymouth. Heavily damaged in the Second World War, it reopened for the league's 1945 resumption. Hosted a 1977 Cup Winners' Cup tie between Manchester United and Saint-Etienne. Record attendance: 43596, set in 1936 against Aston Villa.
_facts: Hosted 1977 Cup Winners' Cup tie, Man Utd v Saint-Etienne

w: Home of Partick Thistle since 1909, also known as Wyre Stadium at Firhill for sponsorship. Seats 10102 in Glasgow's Maryhill area. Has ground-shared with Clyde, Hamilton Academical and Queen's Park, hosted the 2000 Rugby League World Cup, and was home to Glasgow Warriors rugby union between 2007 and 2012.
_facts: Hosted 2000 Rugby League World Cup matches

w: Indoor sports venue in Innsbruck, part of the OlympiaWorld Innsbruck complex alongside the Tivoli Stadion Tirol. Designed by architect Hans Buchrainer, it opened in November 1963 and was renovated 2001-2004. Holds 8000 spectators in the grandstands, up to 4000 more on the playing field, plus an outdoor ice rink.
_facts: Capacity 8000 grandstand, up to 4000 more on the floor
Part of the OlympiaWorld Innsbruck complex
Includes an outdoor artificial ice rink

w: Aquatics complex in Budapest, officially the Duna Arena and unofficially known as the Dagaly Budapest Aquatics Complex. Designed by architect Marcell Ferenc, it was built between 2015 and 2017 as a purpose-built swimming and water sports venue on the Danube's banks.
_facts: Aquatics complex, also called Duna Arena

w: Former stadium in Paris's 19th arrondissement, built August 1918 and named for Robert Bergeyre, a French rugby player killed in World War I aged 20. Home of the Olympique Paris football club, it also staged rugby, athletics and 1924 Olympic football and rugby matches, before demolition in 1926.
_facts: Hosted 1924 Summer Olympics football and rugby matches
Home of Olympique Paris football club
Demolished 1926; area still named Butte Bergeyre

w: Stade Pierre de Coubertin is a multi-purpose stadium in Cannes, France, that opened in 1937. Used mostly for football, it has served as the home ground of AS Cannes since then. The stadium is named after Pierre de Coubertin, founder of the modern Olympic Games, and today holds 9819 spectators.
_facts: Named after Pierre de Coubertin, Olympics founder

w: Home of Liga I club Rapid Bucuresti since opening in March 2022, known as the Superbet Arena-Giulesti for sponsorship. Built for 67 million euro in the Giulesti neighbourhood, replacing the old Giulesti-Valentin Stanescu Stadium. Seats 14047 and hosted the 2022 Cupa Romaniei final.
_facts: Home of Rapid Bucuresti since March 2022

w: Home ground of Boreham Wood Football Club in Hertfordshire, sponsored as the Mangata Developments Stadium Meadow Park. Also hosts Arsenal's youth teams and select women's team matches. The wider Meadow Park public park includes play areas, tennis courts, football pitches and a wildflower meadow.
s: Boreham Wood's ground and Arsenal academy base
_facts: Home of Boreham Wood Football Club
Also used by Arsenal youth and women's teams
Set within the wider Meadow Park public park

w: Home of EFL League Two club Barnet, built on the former Prince Edward Playing Fields in Canons Park near Edgware. Also hosted Tottenham Hotspur Women from 2019 to 2022 and is home to London Bees. Official capacity 6500; record attendance 6215, set in a 3-3 draw with Brentford on 28 January 2019.
